n: This lecture is devoted to section 1.3: synthetic narcotic analgesics, that is dionine, heroin and apomorphine, and the methods of isolating and analysing them. Key terms: dionine, that is ethylmorphine; heroin, that is diacetylmorphine; 6-monoacetylmorphine, in short 6-MAM; apomorphine; Marquis reagent; Rf and UV and IR spectra. The outline is as follows: first we look at the general colours and chromatography of opiates, then dionine, then heroin, and finally we study apomorphine.

Opiates are agents similar in structure to morphine and obtained from it. They include morphine, codeine and the semisynthetic products of morphine. Heroin, that is diacetylmorphine, and its main metabolite 6-monoacetylmorphine are also among the opiates. Heroin is a potent narcotic drug, synthesised from morphine by an acetylation reaction. The diagram shows that morphine and codeine are natural, heroin and dionine are semisynthetic, and 6-MAM is a metabolite.

Now let us compare the origin of dionine, heroin and apomorphine. None of the three occurs in opium or omnopon. Dionine is obtained semisynthetically, by attaching ethyl alcohol to morphine. Heroin is also made from morphine by semisynthesis, through acetylation. Apomorphine is obtained by heating morphine under high pressure in the presence of hydrochloric acid. Remember: all three substances are formed mainly from morphine, and are absent from natural raw material.

t: Colours of opiates with Marquis reagent (1)
n: Marquis reagent sorts opiates into groups by colour. Those giving a red-violet colour are morphine, heroin, opium, benzylmorphine, dihydromorphine and thebaine. Those giving a violet colour are codeine, diamorphine, buprenorphine, dihydrocodeine, morphylong, 6-monoacetylmorphine, normorphine and pholcodine. A blue-violet colour is characteristic of neopine. Because these colours are close to one another, one cannot rely on this reaction alone, and the analysis is supplemented by other methods.

t: Colours of opiates with Marquis reagent (2)
n: With Marquis reagent some substances give yellow and grey tints. Acetorphine and etorphine form a bluish green-yellow-brown colour. Hydromorphone gives yellow-red-violet, and oxycodone and hydrocodone give yellow-brown-violet. The table also shows that ethylmorphine and norcodeine give yellow-violet, and buprenorphine and oxymorphone grey-violet. So the tint of the colour is an important sign in distinguishing substances.

The third table gives the Rf values of opiates on Silufol and Sorbfil plates in three systems. The values are written in the order morphine, codeine and heroin. Heroin has the highest Rf, that is, it rises furthest on the plate. In the methanol-ammonia system, the Rf values of morphine and codeine come out the same, so in this system they cannot be distinguished from each other. The systems are: ether-ethanol-25% ammonia 6:3:1, methanol-25% ammonia 100:1.5 and ethyl acetate-methanol-ammonia 17:2:1.

The fifth table gives the ultraviolet maxima of the substances in 0.1 M HCl. At 273 nm oxycodone absorbs, and at 278 nm dextromethorphan and pentazocine. At 279 nm racemorphan, levorphanol and heroin give maxima, and at 280 nm hydrocodone and hydromorphone. At 281 nm naloxone, naltrexone and oxymorphone absorb. As can be seen, the maxima are very close to one another, so this method is used together with other data.

Let us look at the Rf values on a Silufol plate by system. In the diethyl ether-ethanol-25% ammonia 6:3:1 system, morphine is 0.30, codeine 0.60, heroin 0.80. In the methanol-25% ammonia 100:1.5 system, morphine is 0.37, codeine 0.37, heroin 0.40. In the ethyl acetate-methanol-25% ammonia 17:2:1 system, morphine is 0.20, codeine 0.40, heroin 0.52. We see that in all three systems heroin has the highest Rf.

Now the same three substances on a Sorbfil plate. In the ether-ethanol-ammonia 6:3:1 system, morphine is 0.30, codeine 0.45, heroin 0.60. In the methanol-ammonia 100:1.5 system, morphine is 0.29, codeine 0.29, heroin 0.43. In the ethyl acetate-methanol-ammonia 17:2:1 system, morphine is 0.27, codeine 0.49, heroin 0.65. As on Silufol, here too morphine and codeine give the same value in methanol-ammonia, while heroin lies higher.

The fifth table continued, maxima in 0.1 M HCl. At 283 nm, dihydroxycodeine and pholcodine. At 284 nm, acetylcodeine, acetorphine, benzylmorphine, nalbuphine, thebaine and ethylmorphine. At 285 nm codeine, morphine, nalorphine and normorphine absorb, and at 286 nm buprenorphine. At 287 nm 6-monoacetylmorphine absorbs, and at 289 nm etorphine. Remember: morphine and codeine give a maximum at the same 285 nm.

In an alkaline medium, 0.1 M NaOH, the maxima lie differently. Heroin 299 nm, hydromorphone 290, naltrexone 293, oxymorphone 292, nalbuphine 297, morphine 298. Some substances give two maxima: pentazocine 240 and 300, racemorphan and levorphanol 240 and 299, nalorphine 251 and 298. Buprenorphine absorbs at 300 nm, etorphine at 302 nm, and ethylmorphine at 281 nm. Comparing the spectra in acid and alkaline media together gives a more reliable result.

Tables 7 and 8 give retention times in the HPLC and GLC methods, with the time in absolute minutes. In HPLC the absorption maximum is 279 nm for heroin, 281 nm for morphine and 281 nm for codeine. The retention time of heroin is 4.68 minutes in HPLC and 11.81 minutes in GLC. For morphine, 2.86 and 9.73, and for codeine, 4.11 and 8.38 minutes. In GLC, heroin emerges last.

Let us compare the elution order. In HPLC morphine emerges first, at 2.86 minutes, then codeine at 4.11 and heroin at 4.68 minutes. In GLC codeine comes first, at 8.38 minutes, then morphine at 9.73 and heroin at 11.81 minutes. In both methods heroin emerges last, while the positions of morphine and codeine are interchanged. This difference is important so as not to confuse the substances in the analysis.

Dionine is ethylmorphine hydrochloride. It consists of transparent prismatic colourless crystals, odourless and bitter in taste. Its melting point is 93°C. It dissolves well in water at 1:12 and in ethyl alcohol, and poorly in organic solvents. In the malaka material its solubility in ethyl alcohol is given as 1:25. That is, dionine is a substance that dissolves well in polar solvents and poorly in organic ones.

The action of dionine is similar to codeine. It is used in treating cough and, in ophthalmology, as drops and ointment. Its analgesic action resembles codeine, but it has no narcotic action, and its toxic action is higher than that of codeine. The maximum single dose is 0.03 g. Its metabolism is also similar to codeine. For isolation, acidified water or alcohol is used, and in an alkaline medium it is extracted with organic solvents.

Colour reactions are used to identify dionine. With general precipitating reagents it forms precipitates similar to codeine. Fröhde reagent, that is a solution of ammonium molybdate in concentrated H2SO4, gives a dirty blue colour. With Marquis reagent a green colour appears first, then blue, and finally violet; in this it differs from the opium alkaloids. Unlike morphine, it forms no colour with iron(III) chloride.

Confirmation of dionine proceeds step by step. To the residue of the chloroform extract obtained from the alkaline medium, 0.1 M HCl and 5% mercury(II) chloride are added, and under the microscope colourless thin prisms are seen. In the UV spectrum, a solution in 0.2 M sulphuric acid gives a maximum at 289 nm. In the IR spectrum, on a KBr disc, absorption is observed in the regions of 1064, 1045, 1129, 1499, 1185 and 1264 cm-1. The quantity is determined from a solution in 0.2 N sulphuric acid by UV spectrophotometry, or by GLC and HPLC.

Now heroin. Heroin, that is diacetylmorphine, is a powder of colourless prismatic crystals. It is insoluble in water and readily soluble in alcohol, ether and chloroform. It forms salts with acids. The melting point of heroin as the base is 173°C. Remember: heroin is insoluble in water, so it can be isolated with organic solvents.

Heroin is a very strongly toxic substance. It acts on the body like morphine, but more strongly. Its power to paralyse the respiratory centre and sensory nerve endings is five times that of morphine. If taken often, a person becomes habituated and may fall ill with morphinism, and freeing someone from heroin addiction is harder than weaning them off morphine. Because of its adverse properties, heroin is no longer used in medicine.

Heroin hydrolyses very rapidly in an alkaline medium and in the body. First monoacetylmorphine forms, and finally morphine. The chain is: heroin, that is diacetylmorphine, then 6-monoacetylmorphine, then morphine. Therefore in heroin poisoning, it is mainly monoacetylmorphine and morphine that are found in the physical evidence. That is, heroin itself is hard to find, and its traces remain in the metabolites.

The general rule for identifying heroin is as follows. In the body, in cadaver organs and in extracting an alkaline solution with chloroform, heroin undergoes hydrolysis and forms morphine. Therefore the identification reactions are the same as those for morphine. If a powder or heroin solutions have been submitted as physical evidence, separate reactions are used: Marquis, Fröhde, FeCl3 and H2PtCl6.

Reactions for heroin as a powder or solution. With Marquis reagent a violet colour forms at once. With Fröhde reagent it gives a violet colour, like morphine, and in this it differs from codeine. With iron(III) chloride, unlike morphine, it gives no colour. With H2PtCl6 yellow needles form, with a sensitivity of 0.05-0.07 µg. If the acetic acid formed in hydrolysis is heated with ethyl alcohol and H2SO4, the smell of ethyl acetate appears.

t: Heroin: reactions for powder and solution
n: Let us look once more at the reactions confirming heroin. Marquis reagent, that is formaldehyde and concentrated H2SO4, gives a violet colour with heroin at once. With hexachloroplatinic acid H2PtCl6, yellow needle-shaped microcrystals appear, with a sensitivity of 0.05-0.07 µg of heroin. The acetic acid formed in hydrolysis, when heated with ethyl alcohol and concentrated H2SO4, gives the smell of ethyl acetate. Fröhde gives a violet colour, whereas FeCl3 gives no colour.

t: Distinguishing morphine, codeine, dionine and heroin
n: Two reactions suffice to distinguish morphine, codeine, dionine and heroin. Morphine gives a bluish-green colour with iron(III) chloride, owing to its free phenolic hydroxyl. Codeine, dionine and heroin give no colour with iron(III) chloride. With Fröhde reagent, codeine and dionine give a dirty blue colour and heroin a violet one. So FeCl3 singles out morphine, and Fröhde reagent separates heroin from codeine and dionine.

Spectra of heroin. In the UV spectrum, a solution in 0.1 M HCl absorbs maximally at 279 nm, and a solution in 0.1 M alkali at 299 nm. In the IR spectrum, on a KBr disc, absorption is observed in the regions of 1245, 1764, 1178, 1215, 911 and 1736 cm-1. At present heroin is identified by GLC, GC-MS and immunobiological methods.

Quantitative determination of heroin. Heroin or its metabolites 6-monoacetylmorphine and morphine are determined by GC-MS and HPLC-MS. These substances are also quantified by enzyme immunoassay methods. In general, the quantity of heroin is determined by physicochemical methods. The diagram shows two groups: chromatography-mass spectrometry methods and the immunological method.

Now apomorphine. Apomorphine is poorly soluble in water and readily soluble in organic solvents, and its aqueous solution is alkaline. With acids it forms salts that dissolve well in water, and the hydrochloride is used in medicine. The hydrochloride is a white or yellowish powder, readily soluble in water and ethyl alcohol, and insoluble in ether and chloroform. That is, the solubility properties of the base and the salt are the opposite of each other.

The apomorphine molecule is very unstable. Because it contains two phenolic hydroxyl groups, it oxidises quickly. In air or under the action of oxidants it turns bluish black and loses its pharmacological action. This may also happen when a biological specimen is extracted with chloroform. Therefore, if the chloroform layer is blue-black, apomorphine is tested for first.

Apomorphine is a strongly toxic substance. Because it stimulates the vomiting centre, in poisoning it is injected as an emetic, and also as an expectorant. It is also used to induce an aversion to alcohol in patients with chronic alcoholism. Remember: apomorphine has no analgesic or narcotic action, and in this it differs fundamentally from heroin.

A person poisoned with apomorphine vomits, so deaths are rare: with the vomit, a large part of the poison is expelled. However, the body quickly weakens, cardiac activity is depressed, and arrhythmia is seen. The highest amount that can be taken at one time is 0.005 g. In metabolism it combines with glucuronic acid and is excreted in the urine mainly as glucuronides, in part unchanged.

t: Isolating apomorphine and objects of examination
n: Apomorphine is extracted from aqueous extracts with organic solvents in acid and alkaline media. Examination for apomorphine is carried out only on the instruction of the judicial authorities. Vomit, internal organs, powder or residues of a used solution are sent to the chemical-toxicological laboratory as physical evidence. We see this sequence in the diagram: the specimen, extraction, then the condition - the instruction of the judicial authorities.

Colour reactions of apomorphine. With alkaloid precipitating reagents it forms amorphous precipitates. In the Pellagri reaction, with 10% Na2CO3 and an alcoholic solution of iodine, a green colour appears, and the ether layer takes on a red-crimson colour. The table also gives reactions with acids: with concentrated HNO3, pink and then red-brown; with concentrated H2SO4, pink and then blood-red. With Fröhde reagent, dirty green; with Marquis, pink, quickly turning dirty green.

Let us recall once more the reactions of apomorphine with acids and special reagents. With concentrated nitric acid, a pink colour forms first, then red-brown. With concentrated sulphuric acid, first pink, then blood-red. With Fröhde reagent, dirty green; with Marquis reagent, a pink colour appears first and quickly turns dirty green. This change of colour is characteristic of apomorphine.

t: Apomorphine: iron(III) chloride, UV and IR
n: The residue is dissolved in dilute HCl and dried, then dissolved in water; if 0.1% FeCl3 is added, a blue colour forms, which may then change to red-pink, pink and black. In the UV spectrum, a solution in 0.1 M sulphuric acid gives a maximum at 273 nm and a shoulder at 305 nm. In the IR spectrum, on a KBr disc, absorption is observed in the regions of 1265, 1460, 792 and 985 cm-1. The quantity is determined from a solution in 0.1 M sulphuric acid by UV spectrophotometry or HPLC.

The Pellagri reaction is an important way of identifying apomorphine. After the chloroform extract is evaporated, the residue is dissolved in water. To it are added a 10% solution of sodium carbonate and an alcoholic solution of iodine. If apomorphine is present, a green colour forms. If the mixture is shaken with diethyl ether, a red-crimson colour appears in the ether layer, while the aqueous layer retains the green colour.

To conclude. Dionine, heroin and apomorphine are obtained from morphine semisynthetically and do not occur in opium or omnopon. Heroin hydrolyses to give monoacetylmorphine and morphine, and these are mainly what is found in the specimen. The colours, that is Marquis, Fröhde and FeCl3, as well as TLC, HPLC, GLC, UV and IR spectra and GC-MS, confirm the identification. Apomorphine is distinguished by its tendency to oxidise.

Review questions, part one. First question: explain the metabolism of heroin and the methods of its chemical analysis; what are its narcological and toxicological significance? Second question: explain the metabolism of dionine and the methods of chemical and physicochemical analysis. Third question: how is the analysis of heroin carried out by physicochemical methods?

Review questions, part two. First question: explain the metabolism, analytical methods and narcological significance of apomorphine. Second question: morphine was found when a person's blood plasma was analysed; what situation does this explain? Third, a case: monoacetylmorphine was found in the internal organs of a cadaver. Which substances should be analysed for? Solution: the finding is 6-MAM, the source is hydrolysis of heroin, and the substances to be tested are morphine, heroin, codeine, dionine and other opiates; the conclusion is the likelihood of heroin use, which must be confirmed by additional methods.
